info.title: Where to find system log files?

abstract.para: &productnameshort; logs several types of messages, for example, from the kernel, &selnx; or other services.

topic.para: The following list provides an overview of all system log files found in &productnameshort; after a default installation. Depending on your installation scope, /var/log also contains log files from other services and applications not listed here. Some files and directories described below are placeholders and are only used when the corresponding application is installed. Most log files are only visible for the user &rootuser;. Usually, you can view these files using an editor as they are in plain text.

important.title: Unsupported log files
important.para: utmp, wtmp and lastlog have been removed from &productnameshort; and are no longer supported. If there are any applications that write into these log files, remember that the log files are incomplete then. wtmp has been replaced with wtmpdb, lastlog with lastlog2.

listitem.para: Logs from the audit framework, including &selnx; access control decisions.

Messages logged during the current boot, mirroring what is also shown on the console while the system starts up. boot.msg and boot.omsg are the corresponding raw kernel ring buffer dumps (the same content dmesg shows) from the current and previous boot, respectively—useful when you need the exact kernel command line a boot used.

Logs from the Network Time Protocol daemon (&chrony;). This directory is empty by default. Files only appear here once you enable specific logging directives (for example, log measurements) in /etc/chrony.conf.
Access and error logs of the Common Unix Printing System (cups).

firewall catches kernel-level packet-filter messages. firewalld holds errors and warnings from the firewalld daemon itself. Neither is the place to look for logged network traffic unless you have explicitly enabled that in your firewall rules.
The &systemd; journal's own storage location. See .
Log files from the Kerberos network authentication system. Empty unless you have installed and configured Kerberos client or server tools.

Messages logged to the local0 through local7 facilities, commonly used by third-party applications that do not have a dedicated log file of their own. This file only appears once something logs to one of these facilities.
Mail server logs, split by severity. Empty unless a mail transfer agent such as postfix is installed.
The default destination for kernel and system log messages, forwarded from the journal by rsyslog. Together with /var/log/warn, this should be the first place to look in case of problems.

Log of the update-bootloader tool (also known as pbl), which configures the boot loader on &productnameshort;. Check this file after a kernel update or a manual boot loader change if the system does not boot as expected.
Logs from Performance Co-Pilot, installed and enabled by default for system performance monitoring.
Log of snapper, the tool that manages Btrfs snapshots. Check this file if a scheduled snapshot did not run or a snapshot could not be deleted.
All system warnings and errors, filtered from /var/log/messages.
libzypp log files. Refer to these files for the package installation history.
Logs from the command-line installer zypper.
